examples.title: Three unlabelled samples
examples.situation: A tray holds samples A, B and C, but the trainer has not disclosed identities.
reasoning: Record grit, smoothness, stickiness, ball and ribbon for each after consistent moistening.
Make tentative sandy/clay/loamy group identifications and state uncertainty.
Check precise texture by a validated method if a subgroup matters; drainage and fertility need separate observations.
examples.takeaway: No actual identities are pre-filled; the trainer verifies the learner's observations.

examples.title: Nine conditional candidates
examples.situation: The workshop asks for at least three crops per sandy, clay and loamy group.
reasoning: For well-drained, adequately irrigated sandy soil: carrots, radishes and potatoes from the source model, each checked for depth/water/nutrients.
For structured, drained clay-rich soil: broccoli, cabbage and kale from the model, each checked for waterlogging and nutrient supply.
For suitable loam: tomatoes, peppers and cucumbers from the source, each checked for climate, pH and drainage.
examples.takeaway: These nine names model reasoning, not a site planting order; alternative defended matches are accepted.

examples.title: A client wants carrots in compacted clay
examples.situation: A root check and field observation confirm compaction and poor drainage.
reasoning: Management path: address compaction and water movement, test a suitable organic input and consider a properly designed raised growing area if justified; do not invent dimensions or mix ratios.
Alternative path: trial a locally suitable crop such as a drained-bed leafy crop or bean only after pH, fertility, waterlogging and climate checks.
Explain cost, water and root-development tradeoffs instead of promising carrots cannot grow in any clay.
examples.takeaway: Two distinct defensible paths, with evidence and an individual explanation.

examples.title: Treat three reports as three cases
examples.situation: A is sandy loam/pH 5.8/low N/low OM; B is clay loam/pH 7.2/high N/high OM; C is silty/pH 6.5/waterlogging-prone.
reasoning: A: carrots and potatoes are plausible with moisture and nutrient management; a high-demand corn crop may be lower fit if low N stays uncorrected, not inherently impossible.
B: broccoli and corn are possible if structure/drainage and other nutrients suit; a deep straight-rooted crop may be lower fit under confirmed compaction.

C: rice and willow are the two source examples, each only conditional on a suitable local species/cultivar, climate and water system. Willow is a non-food tree, not a second verified food crop. If the task is restricted to food crops, this model is incomplete until a second locally justified food candidate is supplied; do not invent one. A waterlogging-sensitive candidate can be lower fit with reasons. Carrots would be lower fit if root-zone waterlogging persists; verify drainage, rooting conditions and the local season before accepting or changing that comparison.
examples.takeaway: Report values stay separate from physical sample identities; every row needs reasons and a missing test.
